To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the kinematics of protein secondary structures, such as α‐helices, β‐turns and β‐sheets, can be described by a few simple geometric parameters.
protein backbone structures are kinematic constructions and that the kinematic parameters that describe them are related to the hydrogen bond geometry.
the geometry of the backbone of protein structures can be understood in terms of kinematic constraints.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the geometrical aspects of protein secondary structure and the kinematic constraints imposed by the formation of H‐bonds.

the backbone geometry of a protein, constrained by H‐bonds, can be described as the result of a kinematic construction.
the geometry of protein structures can be understood and described by simple kinematic principles.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the kinematic geometry of H‐bond stabilized structures, constrained to be parallel to the helix axis, is described in terms of a single parameter α, the dihedral angle at the Cα atom.

the backbone dihedral angles of a protein can be described in terms of a few kinematic parameters that can be easily modifiable to accommodate the nonplanar geometry of the peptide units and nonideal backbone angles.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the kinematic geometry of the protein backbone is the key to understanding the structure and dynamics of proteins and peptides.
the geometry of H‐bond stabilized structures can be understood in a simple and unified framework.

the geometry of the backbone structure of proteins and peptides is a constrained kinematics problem and that the kinematics of the backbone structure can be efficiently parameterized using a small set of parameters.
